transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-06
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Ramirez (Redwood AE), Michael Chen (Redwood SE), Lisa Park (Acme Dir Eng), Raj Patel (CTO), Alex Gomez (PM)

Summary:
Sofia opened with context: Acme is evaluating structured output and function calling for a product that executes downstream actions (ticketing, inventory updates). Michael demoed Redwood's JSON-mode structured output, schema validation, guardrails, and the function/tool-calling flow in both Console and via API. Discussion covered hosted vs dedicated, latency/cost tradeoffs, VPC onboarding, SOC2 and KMS concerns. Agreed next steps: pilot pricing, sample prompt set for regression tests, and a benchmark spike.

Topics:
- Structured output JSON mode (schemas, strict vs permissive)
- Function/tool calling (runtime safety, retries, fallback models)
- Console walk-through + API example for function calling
- Guardrails and monitoring (Optimize suggestions, quality regressions)
- Deployment options: Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private/VPC
- Security: SOC2, KMS, audit logs

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sofia from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, uh we've got Michael, our SE, who will run most of the demo.
[00:08] Michael: hey hi, thanks lisa, raj, alex, appreciate the time. quick agenda: show structured output JSON mode, function calling, then console + api snippets, then talk deployment choices and questions.
[00:26] Lisa: yeah excited, we have a product that needs reliable structured responses for downstream services, if the model outputs bad JSON we get errors downstream.
[00:35] Raj: and we're also sensitive to latency since some calls are in-path, and cost for high throughput, so we'll want to see trade-offs.
[00:42] Michael: absolutely. quick qualification: can you remind us rough qps, avg prompt length, and whether you want in-path latency under 200ms?
[00:52] Alex: we're about 40-60 qps at peak for some endpoints, avg tokens per request ~220, and low-latency endpoints target 150-200ms p50. non-critical batch jobs can be slower.
[01:04] Michael: great, that lines up with what we've seen with other retail analytics teams. ok starting demo — I'll switch to the console.
[01:16] (screen share starts)
[01:20] Michael: here in the console you'll see "Structured Output" mode, there's an option for a JSON schema, and a strict mode toggle. I'll paste a schema that matches a ticket object: id, status, assignee, metadata nested fields.
[01:36] (typing sounds)
[01:40] Michael: note, the runtime enforces schema on the response and will either coerce or fail depending on strictness and retry policy. there is a built-in sanitizer and KV cache that's used for prefixes. oops, i just said K V cash earlier, but it's KV cache.
[01:53] Lisa: how often does the sanitizer change the output? like will it drop keys or reformat?
[01:58] Michael: by default we try to coerce simple misformats -- e.g., single quotes to double quotes, missing commas — then validate. in strict mode we fail and trigger a fallback, which you can map to a different model variant or to a default structured response.
[02:15] Raj: fallback to a smaller model to save cost but keep availability?
[02:18] Michael: yep, smart routing can fallback to a quantized variant or a lower-cost region. you can also route by policy: latency-first or cost-first.
[02:29] Alex: show the function calling flow? we want the model to return a json that triggers our internal API to update inventory.
[02:34] Michael: sure — switching over to function-calling demo. so here's an example request: we define a function schema in the Console or via the API, name it update_inventory, parameters are sku, delta, reason. the model returns a structured call and Redwood will call your function endpoint via a secure webhook, or you can have the call payload delivered to a queue.
[02:55] (Michael scrolls through code sample)
[02:58] Michael: important bits: you can set guardrails so only whitelisted function names are allowed, and redact PII before the function call. the runtime supports retries, idempotency keys, and can PII-scrub using rules.
[03:16] Lisa: curious how we do auth for those webhooks inside VPC? we have strict firewall rules.
[03:22] Michael: for Private/VPC we support customer-managed networking and private ingress. for hosted webhooks we recommend mTLS and token-based auth, we also support pushing to your SQS or pubsub inside your VPC via connector.
[03:34] Raj: security stack — KMS for keys? audit logs?
[03:37] Sofia: yes, we have KMS integrations, HSM available for Private deployments, and detailed audit logs in the Console and exportable via API. we'll follow up with the SOC2 + security pack.
[03:49] Alex: and how do you enforce schema changes? our product evolves schemas frequently.
[03:55] Michael: the Console has schema versioning and rollouts; you can pin a schema to a route and then do canary rollouts with validation against a prompt set. Redwood Optimize will flag regressions if new schema or model causes failures on the eval set.
[04:12] Lisa: can we see an example of a failing response and how you handle it?
[04:17] Michael: yeah i'll force a failure — here i'll set strict schema and send a prompt that produces malformed JSON.
[04:25] (typing, sending request)
[04:28] Michael: you can see the runtime returned an error with a structured failure reason, and the fallback policy invoked a fallback model which returned a sanitized minimal json. it also logged the mismatch to the eval tracker.
[04:44] Raj: nice. do you capture token-level cost in the trace? we need to map cost to route.
[04:49] Michael: yes, per-request token breakdown, per-route cost and latency; Console gives time-series and you can export traces.
[04:55] Lisa: question on latency — you mentioned caching earlier, does that help for our in-path calls?
[05:01] Michael: prefix/KV cache helps a lot for repeated prompts or few-shot contexts, it can cut token cost and P50 by up to 30% in some workloads. but for unique prompts caching helps less. autoscaling and batching settings are tunable per route.
[05:18] Alex: what's the difference if we go Dedicated vs Hosted for this flow?
[05:22] Sofia: Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and lower tail latency, dedicated also isolates your data. Hosted is fastest to get started and simpler, but at very high qps Dedicated can be more economical. Private gives you VPC/on-prem options for regulated workloads.
[05:38] Raj: and pricing for Dedicated?
[05:40] Sofia: i'll include dedicated reserve tiers in the proposal; typical pattern is start Hosted for pilot then move to Dedicated as qps grows.
[05:48] (pause, Michael shows API curl example)
[05:52] Michael: here's an API example for function calling: POST to /v1/generate with schema and function definitions inline, we set response_mode=json and strict_schema=true. the response includes a "function_call" object and the arguments as JSON.
[06:10] Michael: small transcription quirk in logs sometimes shows model names garbled, like we see LLM-quantized vs l l m q.
[06:18] Lisa: ha, that's ok. any customers using this for critical path actions?
[06:22] Michael: yes a couple of fintech and retail customers use function-calling as a strong-guarded path with canaries and human-in-loop for high-risk actions.
[06:32] Alex: monitoring — can we set alerts on schema mismatch rate?
[06:36] Michael: yes, Redwood Optimize has a metric for schema validation failures and will recommend batching/quantization/model changes to reduce cost while maintaining quality. it can also trigger regression alerts tied to your prompt set.
[06:50] Raj: do you support function calling synchronous vs async? we prefer async for inventory updates.
[06:55] Michael: both. you can request synchronous call with the runtime invoking your endpoint inline, or have the call placed onto your queue with an acknowledgement. async is recommended for non-blocking flows.
[07:06] Lisa: how do you prevent the model from inventing function names or params?
[07:09] Michael: we whitelist function names; anything outside that list is rejected. plus schema validation prevents extra keys unless permissive mode enabled. you can also add regex rules for param formats.
[07:22] Alex: what's the fallback if the model fails to produce valid JSON after retries?
[07:25] Michael: options: return structured error, map to a human-in-the-loop, or run a recovery transform using a specialized post-processor model. you can also configure a default safe payload to avoid downstream crashes.
[07:38] (customer asks about bench test)
[07:40] Raj: we want to run a spike with our sample data to measure p50/p95 and cost per 1k requests. can you run that?
[07:46] Michael: yes we'll run a benchmark using your prompt set; i'll propose times in the next email. we usually run on Hosted first, maybe a DEDICATED sim if you want to see tail latency.
[07:58] Lisa: any special setup for private data? we need audit logs for GDPR.
[08:03] Sofia: for data residency and audit we recommend Private deployment; audit logs and retention controls are configurable. we also offer data redaction and the option to keep logs only in customer S3.
[08:16] Alex: competitor question: we've looked at OpenAI function calling — how's Redwood different?
[08:21] Michael: main differences: unified runtime with production tooling (rollouts, per-route cost, Optimize suggestions), dedicated capacity option, and first-class schema/versioning and built-in fallback policies. plus we provide VPC/private options.
[08:36] Raj: any limits on function payload size?
[08:39] Michael: payloads are bounded by the overall token limit of the model and we recommend passing IDs and small metadata then fetching large blobs server-side. the runtime also supports chunking responses.
[08:52] Lisa: can you show the docs or a quick link to the function-calling API?
[08:56] Michael: sure, i've pasted it in the chat: https://console.redwood.ai/docs/function-calling (note: this is a demo link).
[09:04] (short silence)
[09:08] Michael: i want to demo a slightly trickier flow — multiple functions and a decision router. i'll set up two functions: create_ticket and reserve_inventory and show how the model picks which to call.
[09:22] (typing)
[09:26] Michael: here's the response: model called reserve_inventory with sku and delta. since you have guardrails, it verified sku format and we used regex to enforce numeric-only skus.
[09:37] Lisa: what about concurrency limits on webhook endpoints? we have limited capacity.
[09:41] Michael: Redwood can fan-out to a queue and rate-limit deliveries to your endpoint; we also support backoff and dead-letter routing.
[09:49] Raj: anything specific about quantization and structured output accuracy? i heard quantized models sometimes hallucinate more.
[09:55] Michael: in our testing, quantized variants can be slightly less precise on subtle language tasks; for strict schema tasks we recommend using a verified model profile with bit-exact kernels. Optimize will recommend quantization profiles per workload after analyzing your eval set.
[10:10] Alex: what's the on-call experience for incidents?
[10:13] Sofia: we provide SLAs for Dedicated and Enterprise customers, and you can export traces to your pager service; we also have runbooks and we can staff a post-sale SRE onboarding during integration.
[10:25] (Michael shows dashboard with traces)
[10:28] Michael: quick note, sometimes our console transcription of model names can be messy — the internal logs are cleaner.
[10:34] Lisa: ha, that's fine. are there any compliance cert gaps we should be aware of?
[10:38] Sofia: we are SOC2 Type II; we have a roadmap for ISO cert if needed and will include the latest status in the security pack.
[10:46] Raj: great. ok, can you summarize next steps?
[10:50] Sofia: yes — we'll send pilot pricing and dedicated options, security pack, and propose benchmark times. customer to share prompts/data and confirm stakeholders.
[10:59] Alex: one more quick thing: do you have a dry-run mode where we can test function calls without invoking our live endpoints?
[11:04] Michael: yes, sandbox mode can capture the call payloads and replay them, or route to a test webhook. good for validating without side effects.
[11:12] Lisa: and can Optimize run locally or is it only in the Console?
[11:16] Michael: Optimize suggestions come from the Console/Platform and we can export recommendations; some parts of the eval harness we can give you as a repo to run locally.
[11:25] (wrapping up)
[11:28] Sofia: thanks all, we'll follow up with the items we discussed. any final questions?
[11:33] Raj: none from me; excited to try the pilot.
[11:36] Lisa: sounds good.
[11:38] Alex: thanks, bye.
[11:40] Sofia: thanks everyone, bye.
